definition: The gap at the base of a hedge made by the regular passage of a small animal.
exampleSentence: A tuft of fur on the bramble showed where a fox slipped nightly through the smeuse.
etymology: Sussex dialect noun, popularised by Robert Macfarlane in 'Landmarks' (2015); related to dialect 'smeuse/smout', to creep through a gap.

definition: A wave-smashed chasm or fissure cut into a sea-cliff.
exampleSentence: The path skirted a zawn where the Atlantic boomed forty feet below.
etymology: Cornish dialect, from Cornish 'sawan' (chasm, gully); recorded in Robert Macfarlane's glossary of landscape terms.

definition: The thin film of ice that lacquers leaves, twigs and grass when a freeze follows a partial thaw, making a whole landscape glitter in sunlight.
exampleSentence: Dawn lit the ammil and the hedgerow seemed strung with glass.
etymology: Devon dialect, thought to descend from Old English 'ammel', meaning enamel; recorded by Robert Macfarlane in 'Landmarks'.

definition: The habit of acquiring books and letting them pile up unread.
exampleSentence: His nightstand was a monument to tsundoku, six novels deep and none of them opened.
etymology: Japanese, a Meiji-era pun blending 'tsunde-oku' (to pile up and leave) with 'dokusho' (reading books); the 'oku' was swapped for 'doku' (to read).

definition: The leisurely conversation that lingers at the table after a meal is finished but before anyone gets up.
exampleSentence: Lunch ended at two, but the sobremesa carried us, laughing, well past five.
etymology: Spanish, literally 'over the table', from 'sobre' (over) + 'mesa' (table).

definition: A beer enjoyed outdoors, especially the first one savoured in the open air on a fine day.
exampleSentence: The instant the sun broke through, the whole café spilled onto the pavement for a utepils.
etymology: Norwegian, from 'ute' (outside) + 'pils' (pilsner/lager); added to the Oxford English Dictionary as a loanword filling a lexical gap.

definition: A place where one feels safe, at home and from which one draws strength; one's deepest refuge.
exampleSentence: The old reading chair by the window was her querencia after a brutal week.
etymology: Spanish, from 'querer' (to want, to love) and ultimately Latin 'quaerere' (to seek); originally the part of the bullring a bull claims for its stand. Entered English via Hemingway's 'Death in the Afternoon' (1932).

definition: The rumbling, gurgling sound made by gas moving through the intestines.
exampleSentence: In the silent exam hall, his borborygmus was practically a public announcement.
etymology: New Latin, from Greek 'borborygmos', from 'borboryzein' (to rumble) — itself an imitation of the gut's noise.

definition: A queasy, fluttering stomach brought on by nerves; butterflies with an upset edge.
exampleSentence: I had the collywobbles all morning before walking out to give my speech.
etymology: English, dating to around 1823; a 'fanciful formation' (OED) probably reshaping New Latin 'cholera morbus' under the influence of 'colic' and 'wobble'.

definition: A shrewd, utterly unprincipled person, especially a politician who chases office with no regard for party or principle.
exampleSentence: Every election season the airwaves fill with snollygosters promising everything to everyone.
etymology: American English, first known use 1845; probably an alteration of 'snallygaster', a mythical poultry-preying creature of rural Maryland (though that word is attested later, so the link is uncertain).

definition: A person skilled in the art of dinner-table conversation; a brilliant talker over a meal.
exampleSentence: A natural deipnosophist, she could turn a dull supper into the night's best entertainment.
etymology: From Greek 'deipnon' (dinner) + 'sophistes' (master of a craft); from Athenaeus's c. 3rd-century work 'Deipnosophistai', in which learned men converse at a banquet.

definition: A habitual faultfinder who can sour any experience with discontent.
exampleSentence: Travel with a smelfungus and even the Alps will somehow be too cold, too steep and overrated.
etymology: Coined (as 'Smelfungus') by Laurence Sterne in 'A Sentimental Journey' (1768) to mock the relentlessly critical travel writer Tobias Smollett.

definition: A habitually smiling face, or the relentlessly cheerful person wearing it.
exampleSentence: Before coffee I can't bear a gigglemug grinning at me across the breakfast table.
etymology: Victorian English slang, recorded in 19th-century dictionaries of slang, combining 'giggle' with 'mug' in its slang sense of 'face'.

definition: A person who stubbornly clings to a habit or belief even after being shown it is wrong; also, the mistaken notion itself.
exampleSentence: He's a mumpsimus about the apostrophe and will defend his error to the grave.
etymology: From a tale of an illiterate priest who kept saying Latin 'mumpsimus' for 'sumpsimus' ('we have taken') and refused to be corrected; in English use since the 16th century.

definition: The anxious wakefulness in the small hours before dawn, when worries swell out of all proportion.
exampleSentence: At four in the morning, deep in uhtceare, every small problem felt like a catastrophe.
etymology: Old English, from 'uht(a)' (the restless hour before dawn) + 'cearu' (care, sorrow); found in Old English poetry such as 'The Wife's Lament'.

definition: A love of solitude and a longing to withdraw from other people.
exampleSentence: After the week-long conference, a wave of apanthropy sent her gladly home to silence.
etymology: 18th-century English, from Greek 'apo-' (away from) + 'anthropos' (human being).

definition: Fresh hope; a recovery from despair.
exampleSentence: The first warm morning after a long illness filled her with sudden respair.
etymology: English, with a single Oxford English Dictionary record dated to 1525; the positive counterpart of 'despair', from Latin 'sperare' (to hope).

definition: A wordless, charged look shared by two people who both want to begin something but each waits for the other to start.
exampleSentence: Across the table passed a long mamihlapinatapai before either dared to mention the kiss.
etymology: From the Yaghan language of Tierra del Fuego; the 1994 Guinness Book of World Records lists it as the 'most succinct word', glossed as looking at each other hoping the other will offer to do what both desire but neither will begin.

definition: The restless anticipation of a guest's arrival that keeps sending you to the window or door to check.
exampleSentence: Full of iktsuarpok, she checked the street a dozen times before his car finally turned in.
etymology: From Inuktitut (an Inuit language of the Canadian Arctic), describing the impatient excitement of waiting for someone to come.

definition: The bracing shock felt when first plunging into cold water.
exampleSentence: The curglaff of the loch knocked the breath clean out of me before the swim turned blissful.
etymology: Scots dialect, from 'cur-' (a prefix marking something going awry) + 'glaff' (a sudden blast); recorded in dictionaries of the Scots language.

definition: The bowl-shaped hollow formed by cupping both hands together; a double handful.
exampleSentence: He scooped a gowpen of spring water and drank straight from his hands.
etymology: Scots and Northern English, from Old Norse 'gaupn' (the cupped hands forming a hollow); attested in Older Scots from the late 15th century and in Merriam-Webster's unabridged dictionary.

definition: The whirring sound made by a covey of partridges bursting into flight.
exampleSentence: A sudden zwer from the stubble field marked where the birds had been hiding.
etymology: Exmoor dialect, an onomatopoeic term recorded in Robert Macfarlane's glossaries of nature words.

definition: The shimmering, road-like reflection the moon casts across water.
exampleSentence: A silver mångata stretched from the shore to the horizon, as if you could walk to the moon.
etymology: Swedish, from 'måne' (moon) + 'gata' (street, road) — literally 'moon-street'.

definition: A puppet on strings; figuratively, a politician whose actions are controlled by someone pulling the strings behind them.
exampleSentence: Voters grew tired of electing quockerwodgers who answered only to their donors.
etymology: 19th-century English; originally a wooden toy figure jerked by strings, later applied derisively to a politician acting at another's command.

definition: Shimmering with a band of shifting lustre, like a cat's eye or polished tiger's-eye stone.
exampleSentence: The silk shifted from green to gold as she moved, chatoyant in the candlelight.
etymology: French, present participle of 'chatoyer' (to shine like a cat's eyes), from 'chat' (cat).

definition: Glowing or flickering softly, with a gentle radiance that plays over a surface without burning.
exampleSentence: Lambent firelight moved across the ceiling as the logs settled.
etymology: From Latin 'lambens', present participle of 'lambere' (to lick); first used in English in the 17th century of flame appearing to 'lick' a surface.

definition: Having the soft, pearly iridescence of mother-of-pearl.
exampleSentence: At dawn the clouds turned nacreous, faintly pink and blue like the inside of a shell.
etymology: From 'nacre' (mother-of-pearl), via French from Italian 'nacchera', ultimately of Arabic origin, + the suffix '-ous'.

definition: Of grey skies, fog and short sunless days; wintry and misty.
exampleSentence: November settled in, brumous and dim, and the lamps came on by four.
etymology: From French 'brume' (mist, fog), via Latin 'bruma' (winter, the shortest day).

definition: Of or relating to yesterday or to a former time.
exampleSentence: He woke with a pridian headache, the lingering toll of the night before.
etymology: From Latin 'pridianus', from 'pridie' (on the day before).

definition: Feeling sick and seedy from too much eating or drinking; hungover.
exampleSentence: He shuffled crapulent into the kitchen, vowing never to mix wines again.
etymology: From Late Latin 'crapulentus', from Latin 'crapula' (intoxication, the after-effects of drink), itself from Greek 'kraipale'.

definition: Having beautifully shaped buttocks.
exampleSentence: The sculptor was famed for his callipygian marble nymphs.
etymology: Dated to 1800; Latinised from Greek 'kallipygos' (the name of a statue of Aphrodite), from 'kalli-/kallos' (beauty) + 'pyge' (buttocks).

definition: Wandering alone; given to solitary roaming.
exampleSentence: She spent a solivagant summer crossing the hills with nothing but a pack and a map.
etymology: From Latin 'solus' (alone) + 'vagari' (to wander).

definition: Aiming at peace; conciliatory and inclined to smooth over conflict.
exampleSentence: Her irenic tone calmed the meeting just as it threatened to boil over.
etymology: From Greek 'eirenikos' (peaceful), from 'eirene' (peace).

definition: Pleasantly round and cuddly in build.
exampleSentence: A jolly-timbered uncle in a too-tight waistcoat carved the goose with great ceremony.
etymology: 18th-century English; 'timbered' in the old sense of 'built, framed' (as of a body's frame) softened by 'jolly'.

definition: Of, relating to, or happening in the morning; active at dawn.
exampleSentence: His matutinal routine of coffee and birdsong was sacred and unhurried.
etymology: From Late Latin 'matutinalis', from Latin 'matutinus' (of the morning), linked to Matuta, the Roman goddess of dawn.

definition: To gaze longingly and silently at someone who is eating, in the hope of being offered some.
exampleSentence: The dog sat groking at my sandwich with such soulful eyes that I caved.
etymology: Scots dialect (also 'growk'), recorded in the Scottish National Dictionary; of uncertain origin, used of children and dogs begging at the table.

definition: To dash about frantically tidying the house in the short window between learning a guest is coming and their knock at the door.
exampleSentence: Her text gave me ten minutes to scurryfunge before she rang the bell.
etymology: English dialect; from 'scurry' (to rush) with an obscure second element, its sense shifting from 'to scour/scrub' to a hasty tidy-up by the mid-19th century. Still heard in Newfoundland dialect.

definition: To laugh loudly, hard and uncontrollably.
exampleSentence: The whole table began to cachinnate until people at the next booth turned to stare.
etymology: From Latin 'cachinnare' (to laugh aloud), an imitative word echoing the sound of raucous laughter.

definition: To leave abruptly and without ceremony; to make off.
exampleSentence: The moment the bill arrived, he absquatulated to the bathroom and never returned.
etymology: A jocular 19th-century American coinage built on mock-Latin lines, riffing on 'squat' to suggest the opposite of settling down.

definition: To hesitate awkwardly while introducing someone because you've forgotten their name.
exampleSentence: I began to tartle at the party, buying time with 'Of course you two know each other!'
etymology: Scots, recorded in dictionaries of the Scots language; an expressive word for the social stumble of a forgotten name.

definition: To give off flashing, glittering points of light; to sparkle.
exampleSentence: Frost made the whole meadow coruscate as the sun cleared the hedge.
etymology: From Latin 'coruscare' (to flash, glitter, vibrate).

definition: In a direction contrary to the sun's course; counterclockwise, traditionally regarded as unlucky.
exampleSentence: Folklore warned against walking widdershins around the old church.
etymology: From Middle Low German 'weddersinnes' (against the way), from 'wider' (against) + 'sin' (direction); naturalised into Scots and English.

definition: In the direction of the sun's apparent course; clockwise, traditionally regarded as auspicious.
exampleSentence: For luck, the bride was led deasil three times around the hearth.
etymology: From Scottish Gaelic 'deiseil', related to 'deas' (right hand, south); the sunwise turn for good fortune.

definition: Early; in good time, before it is too late.
exampleSentence: We rose betimes to catch the tide while the harbour was still grey.
etymology: Middle English 'bitimes', from 'by' + 'time' + adverbial '-s'; in literary use since the 14th century.

definition: Perhaps; possibly; maybe.
exampleSentence: Aiblins he'll come round by spring, once the worst of his temper's cooled.
etymology: Scots, from 'able' + '-ins' (an adverbial suffix); literally 'ably', shading into 'possibly'. Familiar from the poems of Robert Burns.
